rubric: Tokenises with span operations only (an `IndexOf(',')` loop plus slicing, `Split(Span<Range>)`, or the .NET 9 `Split` enumerator) and `Trim`; no `string.Split`, `Substring` or `ToString` on the success path, and the solution compiles on the .NET version the candidate targets.

Parses each token with the span overload of `int.TryParse` / `int.Parse` using `NumberStyles.Integer` and `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`; invalid tokens raise `FormatException`, an undersized destination raises `ArgumentException`, empty tokens are skipped.
`SumAll` streams the input line by line (`EnumerateLines` or manual newline scanning, handling `\r\n`), ignores blank lines and accumulates into a `long` without materialising lines or tokens.

Scratch buffer strategy is correct: at most one bounded `stackalloc` allocated before any loop, `ArrayPool<int>.Shared.Rent` for lines that exceed the cap, `Return` in `finally`, and only the written prefix of a rented (possibly oversized) array is read.

Edge cases pass: empty input, only separators (`,,,`), trailing comma, negative numbers, a line with more values than the stack cap; `Main` runs the examples and the measured allocation over 1,000 repeated `SumAll` calls is 0 bytes.

en.title: String internals

options.text: True, False, True, True
True, True, True, True
False, False, True, True
True, False, False, True

en.explanation: `"hel" + "lo"` is a constant expression, so the C# compiler folds it into the literal `"hello"`; every literal is interned by the runtime, so `a` and `b` are the same object (True). `c` is created at run time from a char array and is not interned, so it is a distinct object (False) even though its value is equal. `string.Intern(c)` looks up the intern table and returns the canonical instance, which is the literal already referenced by `a` (True). `==` on strings is ordinal value equality, so `a == c` is True. "True, True, True, True" assumes that every string with the same value shares one instance; only literals and explicitly interned strings do. "False, False, True, True" assumes that the compiler does not fold constant concatenation and that only `string.Intern` produces shared instances; folding of constant expressions has been C# behaviour since 1.0. "True, False, False, True" assumes `string.Intern` returns a new copy or interns `c` itself; it returns the instance already in the table, and only adds `c` when no equal string is interned yet.

en.prompt: Which statement about `StringBuilder` in .NET 6 and later is true?

options.text: It is a linked list of chunks: `Append` fills the current chunk and links a new one when it is full instead of copying, and `ToString()` copies the characters exactly once.
It keeps a single `char[]` that is reallocated at twice its size whenever it fills up, and `ToString()` wraps that array as the result without copying.
`sb.Append($"{x}")` calls `string.Format` to build the interpolated string first and then copies it into the builder, so it always allocates one extra string.
Below roughly 1,000 iterations the C# compiler rewrites `s += x` in a loop into an equivalent `StringBuilder` sequence, so the two only differ in larger loops.

en.explanation: Since .NET Framework 4.0 `StringBuilder` is a backward-linked list of chunks (`m_ChunkChars` / `m_ChunkPrevious`); chunks grow to at most 8,000 chars (`MaxChunkSize`) by default, although a single large `Append` or an explicit capacity can create a bigger one. Appending fills the current chunk and links a new one when it is full instead of copying everything written so far, and `ToString()` walks the chunks and copies exactly once into the final string; the price is that the indexer and `Insert` may have to walk the chunk list. The single doubling `char[]` describes the pre-4.0 implementation, and `ToString()` has never handed out the internal buffer because strings are immutable and the builder can keep mutating. Since C# 10 / .NET 6, `sb.Append($"...")` binds to `AppendInterpolatedStringHandler`, which formats each hole directly into the builder's chunk; there is no `string.Format` call and no intermediate string, so the interpolated overload is not a hidden allocation. The C# compiler never rewrites `s += x` into a `StringBuilder`: every iteration compiles to a `string.Concat` call that copies all previous characters into a new string, so `+=` in a loop is O(n^2) at any iteration count; the count only determines whether you notice.

en.prompt: Given `string s = "a👍";` (the letter `a` followed by the thumbs-up emoji U+1F44D), what does `s.Length` return?

options.text: 2, because `Length` counts Unicode code points
3, because `Length` counts UTF-16 code units and U+1F44D is a surrogate pair
5, because `Length` counts the UTF-8 bytes the string occupies
6, because `Length` counts the UTF-16 bytes the string occupies

en.explanation: `string` is UTF-16 and `Length` is the number of `char` values (16-bit code units). U+1F44D lies outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, so it is encoded as a high/low surrogate pair (`\uD83D\uDC4D`), giving 1 + 2 = 3. `Length` does not count code points; to get 2 use `s.EnumerateRunes().Count()` (`Rune`, .NET Core 3.0) or `StringInfo.GetTextElementEnumerator` for grapheme clusters. It does not count bytes either: `Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount(s)` is 5 (1 + 4) and the in-memory UTF-16 payload is 6 bytes, but neither is what `Length` reports. The practical consequence is that indexing, `Substring` and `Reverse` by `char` can split a surrogate pair and produce invalid text.

en.prompt: You must produce a 32-character lower-case hex string from a `Guid` on a hot path. Which approach performs exactly one heap allocation (the result string) and writes each character exactly once, with no intermediate copy of the character data?

options.text: `string.Create(32, guid, static (span, g) => { /* write hex chars into span */ })`
`Span<char> buf = stackalloc char[32]; /* fill buf */ return new string(buf);`
`var sb = new StringBuilder(32); /* Append each hex char */ return sb.ToString();`
`return string.Concat(parts);` where `parts` is a `string[]` of two-character hex chunks computed with `b.ToString("x2")`

en.explanation: `string.Create` (.NET Core 2.1) allocates the string with the requested length and invokes the callback with a `Span<char>` over the string's own buffer while the object is still private to the caller, so the characters are written directly in place and nothing is copied; the `static` lambda plus the `state` argument avoid a closure allocation. The `stackalloc` + `new string(ReadOnlySpan<char>)` variant also allocates only the result, but the constructor copies the 32 chars from the stack buffer into the new string, so the data is written twice; it is a good option when the length is not known up front, but it is not the one asked for. `StringBuilder` allocates the builder object and its chunk array, and `ToString()` copies the chunk into a new string, so that is three allocations and two writes per character. `string.Concat(parts)` allocates a two-character string per byte (16 strings plus the array) before concatenating them into the result.

en.prompt: Explain why `System.String` is immutable in .NET and what the runtime and the BCL gain from it. Then describe how string interning works (compile-time literals versus `string.Intern` at run time), what the lifetime of an interned string is, and when calling `string.Intern` in application code is a mistake. Finally, state what immutability costs and how hot paths mitigate that cost.
rubric: States concrete benefits of immutability: instances can be shared freely across threads and by interning without defensive copies, and their hash code and value are stable while used as dictionary keys or in security-sensitive values such as paths, URIs and connection strings.

Distinguishes compile-time interning of literals (the compiler folds constant expressions and the runtime interns every `ldstr` literal in a process-wide table, on the Frozen Object Heap since .NET 8) from run-time strings, which are never interned unless `string.Intern` is called; mentions `string.IsInterned` as the non-adding lookup.

States that interned strings live for the lifetime of the process and are never garbage collected, so interning unbounded or user-controlled input (headers, ids, log messages) is a memory leak, and that each `Intern` call costs a hash lookup plus synchronization.

Explains that interning is not needed for correctness because `==` and `Equals` compare by ordinal value (with a reference fast path); it only pays off for identity-keyed caches or a bounded set of heavily duplicated tokens, and only reference comparison (`ReferenceEquals` / `(object)a == (object)b`) or `string.IsInterned` can observe it.

Names the cost of immutability and its mitigations: every apparent modification (`Substring`, `Replace`, `ToUpper`, `+=` in a loop) allocates, so hot paths use `StringBuilder`, `AsSpan()` slicing with span-based overloads, `string.Create`, or interpolated string handlers instead.
en.explanation: A strong answer connects immutability to sharing (interning, thread safety, stable keys and security invariants) and then treats interning as a consequence of it: literals are interned automatically (Frozen Object Heap since .NET 8), run-time strings only via `string.Intern`, and the table is never collected, which makes indiscriminate interning a leak rather than an optimization. The answer should also acknowledge the trade-off, namely that every modification allocates, and name the modern tools (`StringBuilder`, `Span<char>`, `string.Create`, interpolated string handlers) that keep hot paths allocation-free.
